---
title: "Reading the Source Book Without Losing the Mathematics"
---

# A faithful map of the uploaded book

The uploaded PDF is *Algorithmic Puzzles* by **Anany and Maria Levitin**, Oxford University Press, 2011, 280 PDF pages. The book contains **tutorials** (general algorithm design strategies and analysis), **150 numbered puzzles** (easier 1–50, medium 51–110, hard 111–150), **hints**, and **solutions**.

The authors emphasise algorithmic thinking **without requiring programming**. This course maintains that distinction: state the constraints and prove a relationship before showing any code.

## The source's architecture

| Part in the book | Printed pages | What we study |
|---|---:|---|
| General design-strategy tutorial | 3–21 | Search, backtracking, decrease-and-conquer, divide-and-conquer, transformation, greedy and dynamic programming |
| Analysis-technique tutorial | 22–31 | Summation, growth rates, recurrence and mathematical proof |
| Easier numbered puzzles | 32–44 | Precise statements, small cases, invariants, counting, constructions |
| Medium numbered puzzles | 45–59 | More complex recurrences, graphs, elimination and parity |
| Harder numbered puzzles | 60–70 | Information-theoretic limits, optimal planning and deep recurrences |
| Hints and solutions | 72 onward | Check reasoning **after** trying each puzzle |

Printed page numbers above refer to book pages, not the PDF viewer's page numbers; the PDF also contains covers and front matter.

## A guided sequence

1. **Try without the solution.** Spend a few minutes listing known facts, possible moves or small inputs.
2. **Invent a mathematical representation.** Use a state tuple, sum, graph, Boolean condition or recurrence.
3. **Compute a deliberately small example.** Four queens before eight queens; eight coins before a thousand objects.
4. **Prove a sufficient algorithm.** Explain why following your steps gives a valid answer.
5. **Prove necessity / optimality when asked.** An algorithm using 14 steps does not establish that 13 is impossible.
6. **Check the source hint or solution.** Compare assumptions and methods, not merely final answers.

The lesson text paraphrases puzzle situations and develops **new** worked explanations. It does not reproduce copyrighted statements, hint text, illustrations or the book's original solution prose.

## Common mathematical traps

- A demonstrated answer may be a **possible** answer, not the **smallest** one.
- An empirical pattern from three cases is **not** proof for every positive integer.
- An average-case argument is not a **worst-case guarantee**.
- A program finding a solution is not always proof that no better solution exists.
- A formula written without defining the symbols communicates almost nothing.
